etymology: From Latin passio, a suffering or enduring, from pati, to suffer; thus the Passion is the suffering of the Lord Jesus Christ from Gethsemane to the cross.
biblical_def: The Passion of Christ is the appointed course of His sufferings from the agony in Gethsemane to His expiring cry upon the cross, wherein the Son of God, having taken our nature, bore in body and soul the full weight of His Father's wrath against the sins of His people. In the garden He prayed, "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me" (Matt 26:39), and that cup He drank to the dregs. The Passion is no mere example of patient martyrdom but the very heart of the gospel: penal substitution, the just dying for the unjust (1 Pet 3:18), "the chastisement of our peace" laid upon Him (Isa 53:5). In it we behold both His active obedience — His perfect fulfilling of the law for us — and His passive obedience — His enduring the curse the law pronounced upon us — and both are imputed to the believing sinner. Here justice and mercy meet; here propitiation is made; here the wrath that should have burned upon us forever was poured out upon Him in those dark hours. This dictionary confesses that in the Passion of Christ alone is found the satisfaction of divine justice and the only ground of a sinner's peace with God.
webster_summary: The Passion is the suffering of Christ from Gethsemane to the cross, wherein He bore the wrath of God as a substitute for His people. It comprehends His agony, betrayal, scourging, and crucifixion. It is the appointed price of redemption, not a tragic accident.
webster_full: PASSION OF CHRIST, noun. The suffering of the Lord Jesus from the garden of Gethsemane to His death upon the cross.
It comprehends His agony and bloody sweat, His betrayal, arraignment, scourging, and crucifixion, endured for sinners.
"Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God" (1 Pet 3:18).
It requires us to behold our sin as the cause and His love as the spring; it forbids us to make His death a bare example.
Its sanction: by His passive obedience the curse is borne, and by His active obedience the righteousness is supplied, both imputed to faith.
scriptures: Isa 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
Matt 26:39
And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.
For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit:
Luke 22:44
And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground.
corruption_summary: Modern liberalism reduces the Passion to a moral example or a tragic martyrdom, and progressive theology recoils from penal substitution as "cosmic child abuse," thereby gutting the cross of its propitiatory heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief corruption of our age is the denial that Christ bore the wrath of God. Liberal Protestantism, following the moral-influence theory, treats the Passion merely as a moving display of divine love that softens the sinner's heart, with no objective satisfaction rendered to justice. Progressive evangelicals go further, branding penal substitution as cruelty unworthy of God. But Scripture is plain: He was "wounded for our transgressions" and bore "the chastisement of our peace" (Isa 53:5); He was made "sin for us" (2 Cor 5:21) and a "curse for us" (Gal 3:13). To deny the wrath-bearing is to deny the gospel itself.

Rome, for her part, corrupts the once-for-all Passion by the perpetual re-offering of Christ in the Mass, as though His one sacrifice were insufficient. But "by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified" (Heb 10:14). The Passion is finished, complete, and never to be repeated. The principle to recover is this: the cross is a real transaction in which a real wrath was really exhausted upon a real substitute, so that not one drop remains for those who are His.
roots_summary: From Latin passio, a suffering, rendering the Greek pascho, to suffer, used of Christ's death throughout the New Testament.
roots_lines: The English passion derives from Latin passio, a suffering or enduring, from the verb pati, to suffer.
It renders the Greek pascho, to suffer, as in Acts 1:3, where Christ "shewed himself alive after his passion."
The Hebrew background lies in the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53, "a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief."
The word gathers up Gethsemane (agonia, Luke 22:44), the scourging, the crucifixion, and the cry of dereliction.
Thus "passion" names not emotion in the modern sense but the appointed, willing suffering of the incarnate Son.
usage: The Passion of Christ is the very center of the gospel, for there the just died for the unjust.
In the garden the Passion of Christ began, as He took into His hand the cup of His Father's wrath.
We meditate upon the Passion of Christ not to pity Him but to abhor the sin that nailed Him there.

etymology: From the Old English thritig, thirty, and seolfor, silver; the betrayal price paid to Judas Iscariot, rendering the Greek triakonta argyria.
biblical_def: The thirty pieces of silver were the price for which Judas Iscariot betrayed the Lord of glory, the wages he bargained from the chief priests: "What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver" (Matt 26:15). This sum was no arbitrary figure but the appointed price of a gored bondservant under the law: "If the ox shall push a manservant or a maidservant; he shall give unto their master thirty shekels of silver" (Exod 21:32). Thus the Son of God was valued at the price of a slave. When remorse seized Judas, he cast the silver into the temple and went and hanged himself; the priests, scrupling to put blood money into the treasury, bought the potter's field to bury strangers (Matt 27:3-10). In all this the ancient word of Zechariah was sovereignly fulfilled: "So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver" (Zech 11:12-13). This dictionary confesses that even the treachery of Judas and the greed of the priests served the unchangeable counsel of God, who ordained that His Son should be sold, that sinners might be bought back at the infinite price of His blood.
webster_summary: The thirty pieces of silver were the sum for which Judas betrayed Christ, the legal price of a gored slave under Exodus 21:32. The money bought the potter's field. The transaction fulfilled Zechariah 11:12-13 to the letter.
webster_full: THIRTY PIECES OF SILVER, noun. The sum of money for which Judas Iscariot betrayed the Lord Jesus to the chief priests.
It was the legal valuation of a slave gored by an ox under the Mosaic law (Exod 21:32), so that Christ was priced as a bondman.
"And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver" (Matt 26:15).
It signifies the contempt of men for the Son of God, and the deceitfulness of covetousness in the heart of the traitor.
Its issue: the blood money bought the potter's field, and the prophecy of Zechariah was exactly fulfilled.
scriptures: Matt 26:15
And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver.
Exod 21:32
If the ox shall push a manservant or a maidservant; he shall give unto their master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned.
Zech 11:12
And I said unto them, If ye think good, give me my price; and if not, forbear. So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver.
Matt 27:3
Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders,
corruption_summary: This entry faces little postmodern redefinition, though critical scholarship treats the careful citation of Zechariah and Jeremiah as a clumsy invention rather than the sovereign fulfilment of prophecy.
corruption_paragraphs: The critical academy stumbles over Matthew's attribution of the potter's-field prophecy to Jeremiah while the words echo Zechariah, calling it a mistake or a fabricated proof-text. But the believing reader sees Matthew weaving together the strands of both prophets — Jeremiah's potter and field of blood (Jer 18-19, 32) and Zechariah's thirty pieces — under the inspiration of the Spirit, who is the true author of all Scripture and may cite His own word as He pleases.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is the dreadful estimate that the world placed upon the Saviour: the price of a slave, weighed out in coin, for Him whom the heavens cannot contain. Let the redeemed weigh against it the precious blood by which they were bought, "not with corruptible things, as silver and gold" (1 Pet 1:18), and learn how cheaply the world reckons Christ and how dearly the Father loves His own.
roots_summary: The phrase translates the Greek triakonta argyria, thirty silver coins, rooted in the Hebrew sheloshim keseph, the slave-price of Exodus 21:32.
roots_lines: The number thirty (Hebrew sheloshim) is fixed by the law as the redemption price of a gored servant (Exod 21:32).
The "piece of silver" here is the shekel, the standard weight of temple currency.
Greek argyria (silver coins) appears in Matthew's narrative of the betrayal and the priests' remorse.
Zechariah 11:12-13 supplies the prophetic pattern, the despised price cast to the potter in the house of the LORD.
Thus the phrase joins law, prophecy, and gospel in one appointed sum.
usage: For thirty pieces of silver Judas sold the Friend who had washed his feet.
The thirty pieces of silver fulfilled to the letter what Zechariah had foretold of the despised Shepherd.
The priests would not defile the treasury with the thirty pieces of silver, yet defiled their souls with innocent blood.

etymology: From the Aramaic Qayyapha, a depression or hollow; Joseph Caiaphas, high priest in Jerusalem, son-in-law of Annas, who presided over the council that condemned Christ.
biblical_def: Caiaphas was the high priest who held office in the years of our Lord's ministry and presided over the Sanhedrin that condemned Him to death. Being "the high priest that same year," he prophesied unwittingly, saying, "It is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not" (John 11:50). He spake not of himself, but as the apostle records, "being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus should die for that nation" (John 11:51). Thus the apostate priest, intending only political murder, was made the mouthpiece of a glorious gospel truth he neither understood nor believed: that one should die for the many. It was to Caiaphas that the bound Saviour was led (John 18:14), and there the true and eternal High Priest stood condemned by the corrupt and temporal one. Here is a solemn picture: the priesthood of Aaron, grown apostate and ripe for abolition, sitting in judgment upon Him whose offering would forever supersede their bloody rites. This dictionary confesses that the unbelief of Caiaphas could not thwart, but only served, the saving purpose of God, who turns the malice of men to the redemption of His elect.
webster_summary: Caiaphas was the high priest who condemned Christ and unwittingly prophesied that one man should die for the people. He was son-in-law to Annas and a Sadducee. In him the apostate priesthood judged the true High Priest.
webster_full: CAIAPHAS, proper noun. Joseph Caiaphas, the Jewish high priest who presided over the council that condemned the Lord Jesus to death.
He was son-in-law to Annas, a Sadducee, and held the high priesthood by Roman appointment.
"Nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people" (John 11:50).
He prophesied without knowing it, that Christ should die for the nation, yea, for the children of God scattered abroad.
His name stands for the apostate priesthood that condemned the very Priest whom all its sacrifices foreshadowed.
scriptures: John 11:49
And one of them, named Caiaphas, being the high priest that same year, said unto them, Ye know nothing at all,
John 11:50
Nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.
John 18:14
Now Caiaphas was he, which gave counsel to the Jews, that it was expedient that one man should die for the people.
Matt 26:65
Then the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy; what further need have we of witnesses? behold, now ye have heard his blasphemy.
corruption_summary: This entry faces little postmodern redefinition; the chief abuse is the modern tendency to excuse the council and shift blame, blunting the warning that religious office without grace ends in opposing Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Some moderns, anxious to avoid any charge against the Jewish leaders of that hour, soften the guilt of Caiaphas into mere political prudence, as though condemning the innocent were excusable when the nation's peace is at stake. But Scripture lays the deed bare: the council sought false witness against Jesus to put Him to death (Matt 26:59), and Caiaphas tore his garments and cried "blasphemy" against Him who spake only truth. The guilt was real, even as the purpose of God stood firm above it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dreadful possibility of high religious office joined to a heart that hates Christ. Caiaphas wore the breastplate, entered the holy place, and yet condemned the very Lamb his office foreshadowed. Let every man in the church take warning: gifts, station, and orthodoxy of form may all be present where saving grace is wholly absent, and such men become the fiercest enemies of the Son of God.
roots_summary: The name Caiaphas comes from the Aramaic Qayyapha, possibly meaning a depression or hollow; he is named in the Gospels and Acts as the officiating high priest.
roots_lines: Caiaphas renders the Aramaic Qayyapha, a surname of uncertain force, perhaps "depression" or "rock."
His personal name was Joseph, according to the testimony of antiquity; "Caiaphas" was the family name.
He was son-in-law to Annas (John 18:13), and the two ruled the priesthood between them.
He appears in the trial narratives of all four Gospels and again in Acts 4:6 among the rulers who opposed the apostles.
His office, the Aaronic high priesthood, was even then passing away before the true and abiding Priest after the order of Melchisedec.
usage: Caiaphas asked the Lord to swear by the living God, then condemned His true answer as blasphemy.
In the words of Caiaphas the Spirit hid a gospel that the high priest himself never grasped.
When Christ stood before Caiaphas, the shadow sat in judgment upon the substance.

etymology: From Old English tornen, to rend, and Latin velum, a covering or curtain; the veil of the temple rent at the death of Christ.
biblical_def: The torn veil is the great curtain of the temple, dividing the holy place from the holiest of all, which was rent in two from the top to the bottom in the moment our Lord yielded up the ghost: "And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom" (Matt 27:51). This veil had guarded the most holy place, where the high priest alone might enter, and that but once a year with blood (Heb 9:7), signifying that the way into the immediate presence of God was not yet opened while the first tabernacle stood. The rending was no work of man's hands, for it began at the top, descending from heaven downward, declaring that God Himself had torn open the barrier. By the death of Christ the antitype was accomplished: "Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh" (Heb 10:19-20). The veil was His flesh; in its rending His body was broken, and the holiest stood open. This dictionary confesses that through the torn veil every believing sinner now draws near to God with full assurance, the old shadow abolished and the way of access forever opened in Christ.
webster_summary: The torn veil is the temple curtain rent from top to bottom at Christ's death. It signified the opening of the way into God's presence through His broken flesh. The Holy of Holies was thrown open to all who believe.
webster_full: THE TORN VEIL, noun. The curtain dividing the holy place from the most holy in the temple, rent at the death of Christ.
It was rent from the top to the bottom, by the hand of God and not of man, in the hour the Saviour died.
"The veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom" (Matt 27:51).
It signifies that the way into the holiest, once barred, is now opened by the broken flesh of Christ.
Its sense: believers draw near with boldness through a new and living way consecrated in His blood.
scriptures: Matt 27:51
And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent;
Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus,
By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh;
Heb 9:7
But into the second went the high priest alone once every year, not without blood, which he offered for himself, and for the errors of the people:
corruption_summary: This entry faces little postmodern redefinition; critics treat the rending as legend, while the believer beholds in it the divine seal upon a finished atonement and the opening of access to God.
corruption_paragraphs: The critical mind dismisses the rending of the veil as pious legend or dramatic embellishment, since it cannot abide a sign wrought by the hand of God at the death of His Son. But the evangelists record it as sober history, attended by the earthquake and the opened graves (Matt 27:51-53), and the epistle to the Hebrews builds upon it the whole doctrine of access to God. To deny the event is to lose the very key that unlocks the holiest.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the boldness of access purchased at the cross. Under the old covenant the trembling priest entered once a year behind the veil; now every believer, washed in the blood of Jesus, may draw near continually with full assurance of faith. The veil that shut sinners out is forever rent, and to add any other mediator, ritual, or priest is to attempt to sew up what God has torn open.
roots_summary: From Latin velum, a curtain, rendering the Greek katapetasma, the inner veil of the temple before the holy of holies.
roots_lines: The English veil comes through Old French from Latin velum, a sail or covering.
The Greek katapetasma names the inner curtain before the most holy place, woven of blue, purple, and scarlet.
The Hebrew paroketh (Exod 26:31) is its tabernacle counterpart, hung before the ark of the testimony.
The verb "rent" renders the Greek schizo, to split or tear, used of the heavens at Christ's baptism and the veil at His death.
Hebrews 10:20 makes the veil a figure of Christ's flesh, rent that the way to God might be opened.
usage: When the torn veil fell open, God Himself declared the way into His presence forever made plain.
The torn veil teaches that no priest or ritual now stands between the believer and the throne of grace.
Because of the torn veil we enter the holiest, not trembling once a year, but daily and with boldness.

etymology: From Old English claensian, to make clean, and Latin templum, a sacred precinct; the act of Christ in driving the merchants from the temple courts.
biblical_def: The cleansing of the temple was the act of the Lord Jesus in driving out from the sacred courts those who had turned His Father's house into a place of merchandise. At the outset of His ministry He "made a scourge of small cords, and drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables" (John 2:15), saying, "Make not my Father's house an house of merchandise" (John 2:16). Near its close He cleansed it again, casting out them that bought and sold, declaring, "It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves" (Matt 21:13). His disciples remembered the word, "The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up" (John 2:17, citing Psa 69:9). Here the meek and lowly Saviour appears in holy indignation, for the same love that wept over Jerusalem burned against the profanation of worship and the robbing of the poor under cover of religion. This dictionary confesses that the cleansing of the temple displays both the holiness of Christ, who will not endure His worship corrupted, and His Messianic authority over the house of God, foreshadowing the purifying of His true temple, the church.
webster_summary: The cleansing of the temple was Christ's act of driving out the moneychangers and merchants from the sacred courts. He charged them with making the house of prayer a den of thieves. It manifested His zeal for His Father's house and His Messianic authority.
webster_full: CLEANSING OF THE TEMPLE, noun. The act of the Lord Jesus in expelling the traders and moneychangers from the temple courts.
He did it twice, at the beginning and near the end of His public ministry, with a scourge of small cords.
"My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves" (Matt 21:13).
It manifests His zeal for the purity of worship and His authority as Lord of the temple.
Its sense: God will be worshipped in His own house according to His own appointment, not made a place of gain.
scriptures: John 2:15
And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables;
John 2:16
And said unto them that sold doves, Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise.
Matt 21:13
And said unto them, It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves.
John 2:17
And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up.
corruption_summary: This entry faces little postmodern redefinition, though the cleansing is often misused to baptize the worshipper's own anger, and modern worship trades reverence for the very commercialism Christ condemned.
corruption_paragraphs: Men press the cleansing of the temple into the service of every cause, citing Christ's scourge to justify their own indignation in matters where no holy zeal is at work. But His anger was the wrath of a sinless Mediator against the defiling of God's appointed worship and the oppression of the poor; it is no warrant for the carnal temper of fallen men. The act must be read in the light of His perfect holiness, not as a license for human rage.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is reverence for the worship of God according to His own appointment, the regulative principle which forbids us to corrupt His service with our own inventions. If Christ overthrew the tables of those who merely traded sacrificial beasts, how much more will He judge a church that turns the house of prayer into a marketplace of entertainment and gain. Let His people zealously guard the purity and simplicity of worship as the Scriptures prescribe.
roots_summary: From the Latin templum, a sacred precinct, and claensian, to purify; the Greek of the Gospels uses hieron for the temple courts that Christ cleansed.
roots_lines: The English cleanse derives from Old English claensian, to make pure.
The temple here is the hieron, the whole sacred enclosure, including the court of the Gentiles where the trading occurred.
The "den of thieves" echoes Jeremiah 7:11, where the LORD rebukes those who trust in the temple while doing iniquity.
The "house of prayer" cites Isaiah 56:7, the temple as a place of prayer for all nations.
The "zeal" that consumed Him is drawn from Psalm 69:9, a Messianic psalm of suffering.
usage: In the cleansing of the temple the Lamb of God took up a scourge against the profaners of worship.
The cleansing of the temple rebukes every age that turns the house of prayer into a house of merchandise.
Christ's zeal in the cleansing of the temple was the zeal of love, not the heat of sinful passion.

etymology: From Latin prae, before, and existere, to stand forth or be; the eternal being of the Son of God before His incarnation in time.
biblical_def: The pre-existence of Christ is the doctrine that the Son of God was, from all eternity, before ever He took our nature in the womb of the virgin. He did not begin to be at Bethlehem; He who was born there had no beginning. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Of Himself He testified, "Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58), taking upon His lips the very name of the self-existent God. He prayed for the glory which He had with the Father "before the world was" (John 17:5). The apostle declares that He "being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God" (Phil 2:6), and that "he is before all things, and by him all things consist" (Col 1:17). Thus His pre-existence is not a created or angelic priority but the eternal, necessary being of the second Person of the Godhead. Against Arianism, which makes Him a creature; against adoptionism, which makes Him a mere man exalted to sonship; and against every modern denial of His eternal deity, this dictionary confesses that the Son is true God of true God, begotten not made, of one substance with the Father, by whom all things were made.
webster_summary: The pre-existence of Christ is His eternal being as the Son of God before His incarnation. He existed with the Father before the world was and is the Creator of all things. This truth refutes Arianism and adoptionism alike.
webster_full: PRE-EXISTENCE OF CHRIST, noun. The eternal subsistence of the Son of God before His incarnation in the fullness of time.
It affirms that the Word was with God and was God in the beginning, having no origin and no birth in time as to His divine nature.
"Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58).
It requires us to confess Him true and eternal God, the Creator and upholder of all things.
It forbids the Arian and Socinian errors that make Christ a creature or a mere man.
scriptures: John 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
John 8:58
Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am.
John 17:5
And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was.
Col 1:17
And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.
corruption_summary: The ancient Arian heresy, revived in the Watchtower and in modern unitarian and liberal theology, denies the eternal deity of the Son, reducing Him to a created or merely human figure exalted after His life.
corruption_paragraphs: Arianism, condemned at Nicaea in 325, taught that "there was when the Son was not," making Him the first and highest of creatures rather than true God. This error lives on in the Jehovah's Witnesses, who mistranslate John 1:1 as "a god," and in every unitarian scheme that denies the eternal generation of the Son. But Scripture leaves no room for it: He who is "before all things" and by whom "all things consist" cannot Himself be a thing made. The Nicene Creed rightly confesses Him "begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father."

Adoptionism, on the other side, denies the pre-existence by making Jesus a mere man whom God adopted as Son at His baptism or resurrection. Liberal and progressive theology renews this in subtler forms, speaking of Jesus as a man uniquely filled with God rather than God who became man. Against all such, the doctrine of pre-existence holds the line: the eternal Son, who had glory with the Father before the world was, condescended to take our flesh, remaining what He was while becoming what He was not.
roots_summary: From Latin prae-existere, to be beforehand; resting on the Greek en arche en ho Logos of John 1:1 and the "I am" (ego eimi) of John 8:58.
roots_lines: The term joins Latin prae, before, with existere, to stand forth or be.
John 1:1 anchors it: en arche en ho Logos, "in the beginning was the Word."
The verb en (was) denotes continuous being, set against egeneto (came to be) used of created things.
In John 8:58 Christ says ego eimi, "I am," the name of God revealed at the bush (Exod 3:14).
Philippians 2:6 speaks of His being en morphe Theou, in the very form of God, before the kenosis of the incarnation.
usage: The pre-existence of Christ means He did not begin to be at Bethlehem but is the eternal Son.
Arius denied the pre-existence of Christ as eternal God, and Nicaea condemned him for it.
When the Lord said, "Before Abraham was, I am," He claimed both pre-existence and full deity.

etymology: From Old English bodig, body, and Latin resurgere, to rise again; the rising of the very body from the dead at the last day.
biblical_def: The bodily resurrection is the doctrine that at the last day the very bodies of men, both the just and the unjust, shall be raised from the dust and reunited to their souls. It is not the immortality of the soul alone, nor a spiritualized survival, but the rising of the body itself. Job confessed it of old: "Yet in my flesh shall I see God: whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold" (Job 19:26-27). Daniel foretold that "many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt" (Dan 12:2). The apostle Paul, against those who scoffed, taught at length how "it is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body" (1 Cor 15:44), the same body yet glorified, incorruptible, powerful, fashioned like unto Christ's glorious body. "The dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed" (1 Cor 15:52). This dictionary confesses, against every notion that reduces the resurrection to mere immortality of soul or a figurative renewal, that the self-same bodies of the dead shall truly rise, the redeemed unto life everlasting and the wicked unto the resurrection of damnation.
webster_summary: The bodily resurrection is the raising of the very body from the dead at the last day. The same body is raised, though glorified for the just and condemned for the unjust. It is no mere immortality of soul but the resurrection of the flesh.
webster_full: BODILY RESURRECTION, noun. The rising again of the very body from the dead at the general resurrection of the last day.
It is the reunion of the soul with its own body, the just raised to glory and the unjust to judgment.
"And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt" (Dan 12:2).
It requires us to await a resurrection of the flesh, not a bare survival of the soul.
Its sanction: the redeemed are raised incorruptible and glorious, but the wicked unto the resurrection of damnation.
scriptures: And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God:
Dan 12:2
And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption:
John 5:29
And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation.
corruption_summary: Liberal and progressive theology dissolves the bodily resurrection into a vague immortality of soul or a symbol of continuing influence, denying the rising of the very body that Scripture everywhere affirms.
corruption_paragraphs: From the Sadducees who denied resurrection altogether (Acts 23:8), to the Corinthian scoffers who said "there is no resurrection of the dead" (1 Cor 15:12), to the modern liberal who treats the empty tomb as myth and the resurrection as the disciples' abiding sense of Jesus' presence, the same error recurs: the body is left in the grave. But the apostle stakes the whole gospel upon it: "if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain" (1 Cor 15:14). A spiritualized resurrection is no resurrection at all.

Greek dualism, which exalts the soul and despises the body, has long tempted the church to rest content with the soul's immortality and to forget the resurrection of the flesh. Yet the same body sown in corruption is raised in incorruption; the eyes of Job shall behold God; the graves shall give up their dead. The principle to recover is the goodness of the body as God's creation, destined not for abandonment but for glorification, conformed to the risen body of the Lord Jesus Christ.
roots_summary: From Latin resurrectio, a rising again, rendering the Greek anastasis; the "bodily" qualifier guards against the merely spiritual sense.
roots_lines: The English resurrection comes from Latin resurgere, to rise again.
The Greek anastasis, a standing up again, is the New Testament word for the rising of the dead.
The qualifier bodily (from bodig) insists on the rising of the flesh, not the soul only.
Job 19:26 grounds it in the patriarchs: "in my flesh shall I see God."
1 Corinthians 15 expounds it fully: the same body, sown natural, raised spiritual and incorruptible.
usage: The bodily resurrection means the same flesh laid in the grave shall rise again glorified.
Paul defends the bodily resurrection at length against the Corinthians who denied it.
We confess the bodily resurrection of both the just and the unjust at the last day.

etymology: From Old English fullfyllan, to fill full or complete; the consummation in Christ of all that the law, prophets, and types foreshadowed.
biblical_def: Fulfillment in Christ is the truth that the Lord Jesus is the substance to which all the types and shadows of the Old Testament pointed, and in whom they are completed. He Himself declared, "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil" (Matt 5:17). Risen from the dead, "beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27), saying that "all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me" (Luke 24:44). The sacrifices that could never take away sin pointed to His one offering; the priesthood of Aaron pointed to His eternal priesthood; the feasts, the passover, the tabernacle, the kingship of David, all converge upon Him. "For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen" (2 Cor 1:20). This dictionary confesses that the whole of Scripture is one book with one Saviour at its center, the old covenant in shadow and the new in substance, so that to read the Old Testament rightly is to read it as everywhere bearing witness to Jesus Christ.
webster_summary: Fulfillment in Christ is the completion in Jesus of the law, the prophets, the feasts, the priesthood, and the sacrifices. He is the substance of every Old Testament shadow. To read the Scriptures rightly is to see Him in all of them.
webster_full: FULFILLMENT IN CHRIST, noun. The consummation in Jesus Christ of all the types, prophecies, and ordinances of the Old Testament.
It teaches that law, prophets, feasts, priesthood, and sacrifice all pointed to and are completed in Him.
"I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil" (Matt 5:17).
It requires us to read all the Scriptures as bearing witness to Christ.
Its sense: the shadows are abolished by the coming of the substance, in whom all the promises are Yea and Amen.
scriptures: Matt 5:17
Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
Luke 24:27
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
Luke 24:44

And he said unto them, These are the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me.
For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us.
corruption_summary: Dispensationalism, a 19th-century novelty, severs Israel from the church and reads many prophecies as awaiting a literal earthly fulfilment apart from Christ, while liberalism denies predictive prophecy altogether.
corruption_paragraphs: Dispensational premillennialism, devised by Darby and popularized by the Scofield Reference Bible, splits the people of God into two, Israel and the church, and defers the fulfilment of many promises to a future earthly kingdom centered on a rebuilt temple and renewed sacrifices. But this fractures the unity of the covenant of grace and turns back to the shadows that Christ has already fulfilled. The New Testament knows one olive tree (Rom 11), one people, and one Mediator in whom Jew and Gentile are made one (Eph 2:14-16).

Critical scholarship, on the other hand, denies that the prophets foretold Christ at all, treating every apparent prediction as written after the fact or read back into the text. Yet the risen Lord Himself opened the Scriptures to show that they spake of Him, from Moses to the Psalms. The principle to recover is Christ-centered reading of the whole Bible: the Old Testament is not a separate religion nor a deposit of failed predictions, but the promise whose fulfilment is the Lord Jesus, the seed, the priest, the king, and the Lamb.
roots_summary: From Old English fullfyllan, to fill completely, rendering the Greek pleroo, to fill up or accomplish, as used by Christ in Matthew 5:17.
roots_lines: The English fulfil joins full and fill, to fill to completeness.
It renders the Greek pleroo, to fill up, complete, or bring to its appointed end.
In Matthew 5:17 Christ contrasts pleroo (fulfil) with kataluo (destroy or loose).
Luke 24:44 uses the cognate plerothenai, "that all things must be fulfilled" concerning Him.
The idea is rooted in the Old Testament pattern of type (tupos) and shadow answered by substance (soma, Col 2:17).
usage: The passover lamb finds its fulfillment in Christ, our passover sacrificed for us.
On the Emmaus road the Lord showed His fulfillment in Christ of Moses and all the prophets.
The Aaronic priesthood awaited its fulfillment in Christ, the great High Priest forever.

etymology: From Greek skeptron, a staff or rod of rule, through Latin sceptrum; the prophecy of Jacob concerning the abiding rule in the line of Judah.
biblical_def: The scepter prophecy is the dying blessing of Jacob upon his son Judah, foretelling that the rule and dominion should abide in Judah's line until the coming of the promised Deliverer: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be" (Gen 49:10). The scepter is the emblem of kingship and rule; the lawgiver, the staff of authority; and "Shiloh," understood from of old as a title of the Messiah, signifies the One to whom the rule belongs and unto whom the nations shall be gathered. Thus the kingly office was secured in the tribe of Judah, from which sprang David and his greater Son. The Lord Jesus is "the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David" (Rev 5:5), in whom this prophecy is gloriously fulfilled. He is the King whose throne is forever, of whose kingdom there shall be no end. This dictionary confesses that the scepter prophecy is a sure word, confirming the eternal counsel of God to establish His Messiah upon the throne of David, and that all the nations are gathered unto Him as the rightful and everlasting King.
webster_summary: The scepter prophecy is Jacob's word in Genesis 49:10 that rule shall remain in Judah until Shiloh comes. Shiloh is the Messiah, to whom the gathering of the peoples belongs. It secures the messianic kingship in the line of Judah.
webster_full: SCEPTER PROPHECY, noun. The dying prophecy of Jacob that the rule shall not depart from Judah until the coming of Shiloh.
The scepter and the lawgiver's staff are emblems of kingly authority, here fixed in the tribe of Judah.
"The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come" (Gen 49:10).
It teaches that the Messiah should arise from Judah's line, and unto Him the gathering of the people belongs.
Its sense: the everlasting kingship of Christ, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, is foretold and secured.
scriptures: The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be.

I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth.
Rev 5:5
And one of the elders saith unto me, Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof.
Heb 7:14
For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda; of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood.
corruption_summary: This entry faces little postmodern redefinition; the critical academy denies its predictive character and date, while the believing church reads it as a genuine messianic prophecy fulfilled in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Higher criticism, denying Mosaic authorship of the Pentateuch and predictive prophecy alike, treats Genesis 49 as a late composition retrojected to flatter the Davidic dynasty rather than a true foretelling spoken by the patriarch Jacob. But the believing church receives it as the inspired word of God, spoken centuries before David, securing the kingly line in Judah and pointing beyond David to David's Lord. The word "Shiloh" was understood as messianic by the ancient synagogue itself.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the certainty of fulfilled prophecy as a pillar of faith. Long before any king reigned in Israel, the scepter was promised to Judah; from Judah came David, and from David's line, according to the flesh, came Christ, the Lion of the tribe of Juda. Let the saints rest in a God who declares the end from the beginning and brings every word of His promise to pass in His Son.
roots_summary: From the Greek skeptron and Latin sceptrum, a staff of rule, rendering the Hebrew shebet, a rod, tribe, or scepter, in Genesis 49:10.
roots_lines: The English scepter comes through Latin sceptrum from Greek skeptron, a staff to lean on.
It renders the Hebrew shebet, a rod or staff, also meaning a tribe, the emblem of rule.
The "lawgiver" (Hebrew mechoqeq) is the commander's staff held between the feet of the seated ruler.
"Shiloh" (Hebrew Shiloh) has long been taken as a name of the Messiah, "he whose it is," or "the peaceable one."
Numbers 24:17 echoes the figure: a Star out of Jacob and a Scepter out of Israel.
usage: The scepter prophecy fixed the messianic kingship in the tribe of Judah long before David was born.
By the scepter prophecy we know that Christ, sprung from Judah, is the rightful and everlasting King.
When Jacob spoke the scepter prophecy, he foretold the One unto whom the nations would be gathered.

etymology: From the Greek Lazaros, from the Hebrew Eleazar, "God hath helped"; the raising of Lazarus of Bethany from the dead by Christ.
biblical_def: The raising of Lazarus is the great sign recorded in John 11, wherein the Lord Jesus called His friend Lazarus, four days dead and already in the tomb, back to life by the word of His power. To the grieving Martha He declared, "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live" (John 11:25). Coming to the grave, He "cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth. And he that was dead came forth" (John 11:43-44). This was no swoon nor mere recovery, but a true raising of one whose body had begun to corrupt, a manifest display of Christ's sovereign dominion over death itself. Yet the same sign that gave life to Lazarus hardened the Sanhedrin against the Lord, for from that day "they took counsel together for to put him to death" (John 11:53), and they plotted to slay Lazarus also (John 12:10). Thus the giving of life provoked the counsel of murder, and the road to the cross was set. This dictionary confesses that in the raising of Lazarus we behold a pledge of the general resurrection and a proof that He who is the Resurrection and the Life will surely call all His own from their graves at the last day.
webster_summary: The raising of Lazarus is Christ's calling of his friend, four days dead, from the tomb in John 11. It displayed His power over death and His claim, "I am the resurrection, and the life." The sign hardened the Sanhedrin to seek His death.
webster_full: THE RAISING OF LAZARUS, noun. The miracle by which Christ called Lazarus of Bethany, four days dead, alive from the grave.
It was wrought by His mere word, "Lazarus, come forth," in the presence of many witnesses at Bethany.
"I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live" (John 11:25).
It manifests His sovereign power over death and is a pledge of the resurrection of His people.
Its consequence: the chief priests, enraged rather than believing, took counsel to put Him to death.
scriptures: John 11:25
Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:
John 11:43
And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth.
John 11:44
And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go.
John 11:53
Then from that day forth they took counsel together for to put him to death.
corruption_summary: This entry faces little postmodern redefinition; the critical academy denies the miracle as legend, while the church receives it as sober history and a pledge of the resurrection to come.
corruption_paragraphs: The critical mind, ruling out the supernatural beforehand, treats the raising of Lazarus as a Johannine invention, a theological symbol rather than a historical event, since it cannot allow that a man four days dead was truly called from the tomb. But John writes as an eyewitness of glory, recording the place, the names, the weeping, and the stench of death, and the response of the rulers who could not deny the sign and so resolved to kill both the Lord and Lazarus. To deny the event is to call the apostle a liar.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the lordship of Christ over death and the certainty of the resurrection. Lazarus came forth still bound in graveclothes, raised to die again; but he is a pledge of that greater raising, when the dead in Christ shall rise incorruptible. He who said "I am the resurrection, and the life" will speak the same word over every grave that holds His own, and they shall hear His voice and live.
roots_summary: From the Greek Lazaros, a form of the Hebrew Eleazar, "God hath helped"; the account is given wholly in John 11 and 12.
roots_lines: Lazarus is the Greek Lazaros, contracted from the Hebrew Eleazar, "God hath helped."
He was of Bethany, brother to Martha and Mary, and is called the friend whom Jesus loved (John 11:3).
The phrase "come forth" renders the Greek deuro exo, a direct command of the living voice of Christ.
"The resurrection" here is the Greek anastasis, the very life of which Christ is the source.
The four days in the tomb (John 11:39) underscore the reality and finality of the death undone.
usage: In the raising of Lazarus the Lord proved that He is the Resurrection and the Life.
The raising of Lazarus, far from softening the rulers, hardened their resolve to kill the Lord.
Lazarus came forth bound in graveclothes, a living pledge of the resurrection of all the saints.
